newsitem.title: USA: Dollar bounces in range in US,ends modestly weaker.
newsitem.headline: Dollar bounces in range in US,ends modestly weaker.

text.p: The dollar lacked the impetus to break out of narrow ranges, ultimately ending modestly weaker against other leading currencies, foreign exchange dealers said on Thursday.
Dealing floors mostly marked time before the release of critical U.S. inflation data on Friday, traders said.
The dollar pierced but failed to hold above a psychologically important 1.53 mark barrier and, after a struggle, steadily creeped lower to close at 1.5280/85 compared to 1.5301/06 at Thursday's open.

With Japanese trading floors shut due to a national holiday commemorating the 1964 Tokyo Olympic Games, the dollar drifted lower against the yen to end at 111.25/30 yen, below Thursday's 111.33/38 open.
Market players remained confident the dollar/yen exchange rate would not drop below the key 111.00 level despite hitting a U.S. low of 111.05 yen.
"Down at 111.05, we saw some Far East interest to buy dollar/yen. We're not going to break out under 111.00 today," said Brian McClave, a senior trader at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York.
London and European banks were reported selling dollars at 111.30 to 111.20 yen, which pushed the dollar to U.S. session lows against the yen, dealers said.
Dollar traders were nonplussed by an unexpected drop in new claims for unemployment insurance for the week ended October 5 and a smattering of overseas news.

Jobless claims fell to 319,000 in the latest week from a revised 341,000 in the prior week. Economists had forecast a slight rise to 342,000 claims and said the drop was unusual as claims tend to rise, not drop, in the first week of the month.

Press reports of a rift between German politicians and central bank officials over weakening the entry criteria to allow peripheral nations to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999 had little impact on the dollar or mark, dealers said.
Investors hesitated to make large bets ahead of Friday's release of the U.S. September producer price index (PPI) and September retail sales report.
Analysts said surprisingly strong data suggestive of higher inflation would send mixed signals to dollar traders, but overall it would be negative for the currency.
"On the one hand you may have short-term interest rates move up a bit, but it would not be so hot for equity and bond markets," said Lisa Finstrom, a foreign exchange analyst at Smith Barney.

Higher U.S. interest rates usually benefit the dollar as U.S. assets become more attractive. However, a downturn in U.S. equity and debt markets tends to diminish demand for those securities and thus the demand for dollars as well.
Analysts stressed the data would have to be markedly higher than the consensus Wall Street forecast of a 0.3 percent rise in PPI and a 0.2 percent jump in retail sales.
Last Friday, a weak U.S. employment report surprised Wall Street and while bonds and stocks dramatically sold off, the dollar showed little reaction.

"The dollar held up remarkably well after the employment number and it would be hard for the PPI numbers to be as shocking as the employment number," said Anne Mills, a foreign exchange analyst at Lehman Brothers.

In other trade, the dollar slipped to 1.2493/98 Swiss francs from 1.2523/28 at Thursday's open. Sterling edged higher to $1.5663/68 from $1.5653/58. The dollar slipped to Canadian $1.3503/08 from $1.3510/15. -- Roanne Daniels
